vignette: Mara, a 63-year-old Oceania woman and project manager, has been struggling with the aftermath of her life-threatening illness. Married for over three decades, Mara’s daily routine was once filled with planning and managing projects at work and social engagements with friends. However, since her diagnosis, she experiences heightened sensitivity to certain triggers that have fundamentally altered her life. The traumatic event began several months ago when she was rushed to the hospital after experiencing severe symptoms. The memory of being hooked up to various medical machines, needles piercing her skin, and doctors administering life-saving treatments is seared into her mind with such clarity that it feels almost as if she is reliving those moments again each time a related trigger appears. Certain conversation topics about health or illness send Mara spiraling into distress. The mere mention of hospital visits or procedures can set off a flood of sensory memories, where the sights and sounds of the medical equipment come back in vivid detail. She feels her body reenacting the positions it was in during those frightening moments, and this bodily sensation is often accompanied by intense feelings of shame about what happened to her body. The physical presence of needles or other medical equipment at work, such as when a colleague brings in a first-aid kit for an office presentation, can trigger Mara’s memories. The full sensory reliving of the trauma makes her feel as though she is back in the hospital again, and this triggers her irritability and difficulty concentrating on tasks. She often reacts aggressively to these reminders, which further exacerbates her fear and anxiety. Mara had come to believe that her life was destroyed by the illness, and she can no longer trust her body’s signals or its ability to protect her. These negative appraisals have deepened her sense of shame and made it increasingly difficult for her to engage with others without feeling triggered. She avoids medical check-ups and even hesitates to go to her doctor for routine care due to the overwhelming fear of reliving those traumatic moments. Over time, Mara’s body has become a source of constant worry and distress. When someone touches her unexpectedly, she reacts with alarm as if anticipating another painful or frightening experience. Her irritability and difficulty concentrating have strained her relationships both at work and at home. She finds herself withdrawing from social engagements and even avoiding conversations that might bring up memories of the illness. Her husband notices the changes in Mara’s behavior and has encouraged her to seek help, but she is still apprehensive about revisiting those painful experiences. Despite her efforts to maintain a semblance of normalcy, the cycle of triggers, negative appraisals, and threat responses continues to tighten its grip on her daily life. Mara’s memories often feel like they are inescapable shadows that follow her throughout her day. The bodily sensations that accompany these memories reinforce her sense of distrust towards her body, leading her to avoid any situation where she might be reminded of the trauma. This avoidance has led to a significant reduction in her work productivity and social engagement. What frightens Mara most is the fear that her life will never return to what it was before. However, she is also hopeful that with support, she can find ways to manage these overwhelming feelings and regain some sense of control over her life. The cumulative impact of her symptoms has finally brought her to seek help, recognizing that without intervention, this cycle may only intensify further.
